title: Taking the 'Alternative' Out of Alternative Legal Service Providers: Remapping the Corporate Legal Ecosystem in the Age of Integrated Solutions
pub: Prepublication chapter draft; later published in New Suits: Appetite for Disruption in the Legal World (2019) and in adapted form by The Practice
author: David B. Wilkins · María J. Esteban Ferrer

dup.label: taking alternative out alternative legal service providers remapping corporate legal ecosystem in age integrated solutions

sib.t: Taking the “Alternative” Out of Alternative Legal Service Providers

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: In-house power: Business integration risks professional capture
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account of in-house counsel gaining purchasing and diagnostic power, reducing law firms’ informational advantage, and aligning legal work with business objectives. However, it does not assess whether that integration weakens resistance to harmful demands or argue for reciprocal duties or contextual regulation, leaving the cluster’s principal capture-and-response proposition unresolved.
qs: At the same time these increasingly credentialed and sophisticated internal lawyers now act as the company’s “chief legal diagnostician,” determining the company’s legal needs and how these needs fit into the company’s overall strategy and goals – thus becoming a credible “alternative” to the law firm senior partners who traditionally played this “trusted advisor” role (Gilson 1990; Heineman 2016).

This “in-house counsel movement,” as the legal scholar Robert Rosen has aptly labeled this phenomenon, has significantly altered the balance of power within the legal ecosystem by reducing the information asymmetry between corporate clients and traditional law firms (Rosen 1989; Wilkins 2012).

st.t: Legal outsourcing: Commercial growth need not advance workers
st.an: The source explains how LPOs gained legitimacy and began competing with technology firms, but it does not assess outsourced workers’ substantive work, professional capital, autonomy or status. It therefore neither confirms nor rejects the cluster’s principal claim that commercial growth need not advance workers.
qs: Thus, LPO providers actively lobbied bar officials to clear ethical issues, while instituting rigorous controls taken from the business world such as Six Sigma and ISO certification to reassure end users and regulators about quality, confidentiality, and security concerns (Deloitte 2017; Thomson Reuters 2015).

Indeed, these now mainstream players are finding themselves increasingly in competition with an even newer breed of technology firms, ranging from legal tech start-ups to established technology giants, including, once again, Thomson Reuters.

st.t: Competitive strategy: Build-versus-buy becomes a portfolio
st.an: The source accepts the portfolio logic and materially extends it to the Big Four, showing how acquisitions and technology alliances can be combined to build integrated legal, technology and business-service capabilities. It supports the cluster’s account of overlapping provider roles, while offering evidence of strategic intent rather than demonstrated competitive superiority or client outcomes.
qs: The actions of the Big 4 over the last few years make it clear that they are intent on developing a similar set of capabilities.

As Deloitte makes clear on its website, these alliances are meant to co-create solutions to help clients solve “complex challenges \[…\] by combining leading technology with \[…\] time-tested business acumen and strong industry relationships” (Deloitte 2019.

st.t: General counsel: Strategic authority carries guardian tension
st.an: The source accepts that corporate legal departments gained purchasing power and materially develops the cluster’s supply-chain account. It explains how persistent costs—including the fixed cost of in-house lawyers—drove general counsel toward outsourcing, offshoring, flexible staffing and multidisciplinary providers, while technology both enabled unbundling and complicated cost control.
qs: But as legal costs continued to rise even for companies with large and sophisticated in-house counsel departments, the internal lawyers whose initial claim was that they were a low cost “alternative” to traditional law firms began to face increasing pressure to find even lower cost alternatives to using the expensive fixed cost resource of full-time in-house lawyers.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s emphasis on redesign rather than wholesale replacement and materially extends it from task allocation to ecosystem-wide integration, multidisciplinary delivery, pricing and provider-boundary change. It also reinforces that technology must be embedded in organisational infrastructure and that implementation outcomes are uncertain, though it does not directly assess jagged AI capability or verification.
qs: Because software is embedded into the user’s existing infrastructure, legal tech companies are as much partners with law firms and in-house legal departments as they are substitutes for these “traditional” services.
To be sure, it is far from certain that any of the participants in this increasingly complex ecosystem – let alone all of them – will be able to deliver on their promises of innovation and change.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source accepts buyer-led reconfiguration, value-based pricing and competition among law firms, ALSPs and multidisciplinary providers, while materially extending the proposition from workflow disaggregation toward integrated, customised business solutions. It also reinforces the cluster’s cautious coexistence thesis: incumbent law firms remain important if they adapt. It does not substantively address the cluster’s AI-specific junior-training and verification risks.
qs: These forces, we argue, are producing a market that favors “integrated solutions” and value-based pricing over traditional domain expertise purchased on a fee for service model.

st.t: Big Four: Integration matters more than replacement
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s central proposition: competition is shifting toward integrated business solutions and simultaneous cooperation and competition, rather than straightforward Big Four replacement of law firms. It also preserves law firms’ continuing advantages and distinguishes capacity-building from proven implementation success.
qs: Thus, rather than establishing free standing legal networks, each of the large accountancy networks have aggressively moved to integrate their legal offering with their other advisory services to build on their strong capabilities in technology, strategy, project management, and global service delivery.

UnitedLex’s most recent deal with LeClaireRyan further underscores this trend towards what business scholars call “cooption” – simultaneous cooperation and competition – in the new legal services ecosystem (Wilkins 2010).

st.t: Big Law economics: Durable value exceeds firm size
st.an: The source directly supports the synthesis’s principal claim that Big Law is resilient but must adapt rather than facing imminent disappearance. It treats record profitability as evidence against collapse while emphasizing continuing structural pressure on all providers to innovate; its cautions about uneven recovery and subdued growth are consistent with the synthesis’s focus on durability rather than size or headline performance alone.

st.t: Corporate buyers: Insourcing and partnerships coexist
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition that sophisticated in-house counsel shifted purchasing control toward corporate buyers while fostering a diversified ecosystem rather than simply displacing law firms. It describes buyer-led use of outsourcing, flexible staffing and multidisciplinary providers alongside traditional firms’ adoption of alternative delivery practices.
qs: This “in-house counsel movement,” as the legal scholar Robert Rosen has aptly labeled this phenomenon, has significantly altered the balance of power within the legal ecosystem by reducing the information asymmetry between corporate clients and traditional law firms (Rosen 1989; Wilkins 2012).

st.t: Cravath model: Modern firms retain hollowed labels
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core historical argument that the Cravath System became dominant because it was contingently aligned with client and labour markets, and that this alignment later weakened. It does not substantiate the cluster’s more specific account of modern firms retaining Cravath labels while abandoning core employment and governance commitments.
qs: The Cravath System triumphed because it was exceptionally well “aligned” with other key elements of the evolving corporate ecosystem in which these firms operated (Mawdsley and Somaya 2015).
By the latter decades of the twentieth century, however, this beneficial alignment had begun to unravel.

st.t: Firm resilience: High profits may conceal structural weakness
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central profitability paradox: record profits rebut imminent-collapse claims but do not establish universal health or long-term durability. It also identifies persistent technological, global and competitive pressures requiring legal providers to adapt, while framing change as continuing evolution rather than near-term incumbent collapse.

st.t: Firm tournament: Partnership extends rather than ends competition
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s systemic account by explaining the Cravath System’s success as contingent on alignment with corporate demand, graduate labour supply, durable client relationships and credible partnership rewards—not inherent organizational superiority. Its observation that this alignment later began to unravel is consistent with the cluster’s historical qualification, though it does not itself address post-partnership competition in detail.
qs: The Cravath System triumphed because it was exceptionally well “aligned” with other key elements of the evolving corporate ecosystem in which these firms operated (Mawdsley and Somaya 2015).
By the latter decades of the twentieth century, however, this beneficial alignment had begun to unravel.

st.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s business-model framing by arguing that technology, buyer demand and blurred provider boundaries are pushing corporate legal services toward integrated solutions and value-based pricing. It also reinforces the cluster’s measured view that established firms may adapt rather than collapse, though it does not address generative AI’s specific effects on staffing, verification or workflow governance.
qs: These forces, we argue, are producing a market that favors “integrated solutions” and value-based pricing over traditional domain expertise purchased on a fee for service model.

st.t: Provider convergence: Buyers coordinate an unbundled market
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s central proposition that corporate legal delivery is converging around integrated client solutions rather than dividing neatly between traditional firms and an alternative sector. It also aligns with the cluster’s caution that boundary-crossing models do not yet prove hybrid-provider superiority or incumbent displacement.
qs: Similarly, we argue, as corporate clients increasingly demand professional services that are “integrated,” “customized,” and “agile,” the parts of the market that are now considered “alternative” – e.g., technology, managed services, flexible staffing, and multidisciplinary practice – are also moving from the periphery to the core.
Whether ULX Partners will be able to deliver on these ambitious promises, of course, remains to be seen.

st.t: Value capture: Integrated delivery reshapes market boundaries
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s principal proposition that legal-market boundaries are being reshaped around integrated platforms combining legal expertise, technology, talent and delivery capabilities. It treats this as an ecosystem-wide strategic shift involving law firms, in-house departments, vendors and other providers, while appropriately leaving actual success and realised value gains unresolved.
qs: Whether or not these efforts are successful, they underscore that the move toward an integrated solutions model is no longer an “alternative” – and therefore marginal – part of the legal ecosystem.

kp.k: The alternative label obscures an increasingly integrated legal ecosystem
kp.d: The authors’ central argument is that categorizing emerging providers as alternatives marginalizes their significance and falsely treats traditional firms as the default standard. Writing in 2019, they argue that demand for integrated, customized and agile business solutions is moving technology, managed services, flexible staffing and multidisciplinary practice toward the market’s core. Their discussion encompasses software vendors as well as businesses delivering legal work, without establishing that these are identical provider categories.
qs: the very discourse used to cast these new providers as the harbingers of impending dramatic changes in the market for legal services continues to marginalize and mask their true significance.
These forces, we argue, are producing a market that favors “integrated solutions” and value-based pricing over traditional domain expertise purchased on a fee for service model.

kp.k: Reported ALSP revenues and adoption were growing before 2019
kp.d: Citing the 2019 Thomson Reuters, Georgetown, Oxford and Acritas report, the chapter reports ALSP revenues increasing from $8.4 billion in 2015 to $10.7 billion in 2017, with a compound annual growth rate of 12.9%. It also reports that more than one-third of companies and over fifty percent of law firms used at least one of the top five ALSP functions. These are attributed market statistics, not measurements of AI adoption or AI-caused growth.
qs: revenues from ALSPs grew from \$8.4billion in 2015 to \$10.7 billion in 2017, a compound annual growth rate of 12.9%.
more than one-third of companies, and over fifty percent of law firms, reporting that they are currently using at least one of the top five functions typically performed by ALSPs.

kp.k: Historically, today's traditional firms were disruptive organizational alternatives
kp.d: The authors use the Cravath System as historical framework evidence: organized associate–partner firms were initially criticized as law factories but became the professional gold standard by the 1960s. Their success reflected alignment with expanding corporate legal needs, clients lacking internal resources and a plentiful supply of graduates needing practical training. This history supports the argument that provider legitimacy and organizational advantage depend on changing market conditions rather than immutable professional forms.
qs: Ironically, what we now consider to be the “traditional” mode of providing corporate legal services was once itself an “alternative.”

Yet by the 1960s, large law firms following the Cravath System were universally viewed as the gold standard for providing legal services, attracting top talent, and sitting atop the income and prestige hierarchy of the profession

kp.k: In-house counsel shifted purchasing power and diagnostic authority
kp.d: The chapter describes the in-house counsel movement beginning in the 1980s as a shift from simple labor-cost savings toward claims of superior business understanding. GCs became legal purchasing agents and diagnosticians, challenged firms’ trusted-adviser role and reduced information asymmetry. Subsequent pressure on in-house fixed costs encouraged outsourcing, offshoring, flexible staffing and multidisciplinary providers. The authors’ historical ALSP framing here describes buyer-side organizational change, not a classification of corporate departments as external providers.
qs: GCs have increasingly become the company’s “chief legal purchasing agent,” charged with breaking up the long-standing relationships between companies and law firms, and requiring firms to compete for every new piece of significant business.

This “in-house counsel movement,” as the legal scholar Robert Rosen has aptly labeled this phenomenon, has significantly altered the balance of power within the legal ecosystem by reducing the information asymmetry between corporate clients and traditional law firms

kp.k: The financial crisis accelerated adaptation, not inevitable firm extinction
kp.d: The authors reject both predictions of imminent Big Law extinction and the view that the global financial crisis was merely a temporary correction. They cite top firms’ record profitability in 2018 and recovering US legal employment and law-school applications, while noting that employment and applications remained below pre-2008 levels. They attribute continuing pressure to globalization, technological acceleration and blurring service boundaries, while acknowledging protectionism, privacy, security and regulatory constraints.
qs: The fact that many top firms had their most profitable year ever in 2018 (Bruch 2018) underscores that we are not on the verge of “the death of big law”
both applications to law school and legal employment in the United States are once again on the rise – although neither has returned to pre-2008 levels

kp.k: Software competes with labor arbitrage and enables provider partnerships
kp.d: The chapter argues that software increasingly competes with outsourcing-based labor savings, while integration into existing infrastructure makes technology vendors partners as well as potential substitutes for firms and in-house teams. Its Figure 1 discussion draws on a review of two hundred eighty academic papers and professional reports, specifically nineteen discussing technology-company services after the crisis; citation frequency is explicitly a rough proxy for salience, not adoption or performance. Established vendors are described as advantaged by resources, brands and implementation experience, while startups differentiate through AI, machine learning, flexibility, speed and cost.
qs: The percentage of total documents citing particular legal services offered by these ALSP provides a rough proxy of the salience of these services in the legal community.
Software solutions now actively compete with labor arbitrage as the primary mechanism for both companies and legal firms to reduce legal costs.

Because software is embedded into the user’s existing infrastructure, legal tech companies are as much partners with law firms and in-house legal departments as they are substitutes for these “traditional” services.

kp.k: Outsourcing evolves into jointly managed, multidisciplinary legal functions
kp.d: The authors present UnitedLex’s arrangements with DXC and GE, and GE’s tax arrangement with PwC, as examples of deeper integration than task outsourcing. The DXC arrangement involved 150 DXC lawyers becoming UnitedLex employees and 250 UnitedLex lawyers, engineers and project managers supporting DXC globally. The GE–PwC arrangement transferred more than 600 accountants, lawyers and tax advisers, who would continue GE work and help develop products for other clients. Seamlessness is an expressed customer goal, not a demonstrated outcome.
qs: Rather than simply “outsourcing” specific legal tasks, DXC has partnered with Unitedlex to create a unified legal team in which both organizations jointly manage the legal function
including 150 DXC lawyers becoming UnitedLex employees, and 250 Unitedlex lawyers, engineers, and project managers dedicated to supporting DXC globally.
seamless legal services to the business client, regardless of whether the team member is from DXC or Unitedlex

kp.k: Hybrid platforms combine cooperation and competition with incumbent firms
kp.d: Elevate’s acquisitions, law-firm software development and the 2018 UnitedLex–LeClaireRyan ULX Partners venture illustrate the authors’ argument that providers simultaneously collaborate and compete. ULX promised technology, capital, process innovation, management capabilities and improved economics; the authors explicitly withhold judgment on delivery and cite LeClaireRyan partner departures as a warning. They also report the 2019 Thomson Reuters finding that about one-third of law firms planned an ALSP affiliate within five years, distinguishing intentions from established affiliates.
qs: Whether ULX Partners will be able to deliver on these ambitious promises, of course, remains to be seen.
The fact that LeClaireRyan has been shedding partners since the announcement was made underscores that the success of this and other hybrid models is far from guaranteed
about one-third of law firms say that they plan to establish their own ALSP affiliate within the next five years

kp.k: Agile work integrates staffing, technology and cross-functional collaboration
kp.d: Drawing an analogy from software development’s 2001 Agile Manifesto, the authors describe legal adoption since 2008, led by in-house departments using small, self-governing, cross-functional teams. Axiom’s five-year Johnson & Johnson contract-management partnership illustrates movement beyond temporary placements toward technology- and process-supported workforces. Orrick’s flexible-working commitments illustrate incumbent adaptation. The chapter cautions that successful implementation of these promises remains uncertain; agile here concerns project management and working arrangements, not autonomous AI agents.
qs: since 2008, agile project management is increasingly being applied to legal services
creating small, self-governing, cross-functional teams to solve problems and drive results for clients
this trend also underscores the growing interdependence of “staffing” and “technology” in an agile working environment

kp.k: Big Four legal strategies shift toward integrated business solutions
kp.d: The authors argue that Deloitte, EY, KPMG and PwC rebuilt legal networks after post-Enron restrictions by serving non-audit clients and expanding in permissive or reforming jurisdictions. By the chapter’s account, their networks exceeded their 2002 size and had significant presence in major markets except the United States. Unlike their 1990s imitation of law firms, they increasingly integrated law with advisory, technology, strategy and project management; all four had UK ABS licenses. Acquisitions and alliances, including Deloitte–Kira and EY–Riverview, illustrate capability building rather than independently measured effectiveness.
qs: over the last decade the Big 4 have quietly rebuilt their legal networks to the point where they are now larger than they were in 2002.
Instead their goal is to create a new kind of professional service that integrates law into global business solutions
This fully integrated MDP model is now fully legal in the United Kingdom, where each of the Big 4 have now been granted an “alternative business structure” license

kp.k: Client dissatisfaction supports demand for commercially integrated legal advice
kp.d: The chapter cites a 2017 LexisNexis–Cambridge Judge Business School study reporting that forty percent of clients considered senior partners to have only basic business knowledge and seventy-five percent received little help analyzing their legal-work portfolio. The authors interpret these sentiments as supporting the visibility of Big Four offerings and law-firm moves into consulting and advisory services. They also expect buyer-side legal operations specialists and CLOC’s standards-sharing activity to accelerate market rationalization, while acknowledging that much of CLOC’s promise remained unfulfilled.
qs: forty percent noted that senior partners of their law firms appeared to lack more than a basic knowledge of their business
seventy-five percent mentioned they get little help from law firms when analyzing the complex portfolio of legal work given to them
And while CLOC has made great strides, much of the organization’s promise to rationalize the legal services market remains unfulfilled

kp.k: Integrated delivery remains difficult, and firms retain competitive advantages
kp.d: The authors caution that innovation commitments do not establish organizational transformation. They cite difficulties within the Big Four’s tax and consulting businesses and IBM’s own digital adaptation as reasons not to assume legal-sector success. Reporting Dolin and Buley’s argument, they identify specialized expertise, flexible capacity and reputational bonding that reduces search and monitoring costs in high-stakes matters as enduring law-firm advantages. Their forecast is increasing importance of integrated delivery, not guaranteed success or complete convergence.
qs: it is far from certain that any of the participants in this increasingly complex ecosystem – let alone all of them – will be able to deliver on their promises of innovation and change.

large law firms continue to serve an important purpose in providing the kind of specialized services and flexible capacity that led to the original success of the Cravath System, as well as the kind of reputational bonding that mitigates search and monitoring costs particularly in high stakes matters

kp.k: AI displacement is predicted alongside continuing human-capital intensity
kp.d: The chapter predicts that AI and machine learning will replace some legal jobs but that corporate legal services will remain human-capital intensive for the foreseeable future. It provides no displacement estimate, affected seniority distribution or task-level performance measurement. The associated recommendation is to train lawyers to work with technology and collaborate with other professionals, adding technology and data fluency, business literacy and cross-cultural adaptability to core legal knowledge and skills.
qs: Although artificial intelligence and machine learning will surely replace some legal jobs, the delivery of corporate legal services is likely to remain a human capital intensive endeavor for the foreseeable future.

this will require law schools to teach a broad range of “complimentary competencies” – technology and data fluency, business literacy, cross cultural adaptability – along with core legal knowledge and skills to their graduates

kp.k: Evidence-based regulation must preserve rule-of-law obligations beyond market efficiency
kp.d: The authors recommend evaluating traditional, alternative and hybrid delivery models on evidence rather than categorical professional distinctions or blanket core-values rhetoric. However, they reject leaving predictability, fairness and individual rights solely to market forces. Their normative conclusion is that providers should deliver client solutions while preserving the rule of law, and that powerful corporate clients should be encouraged to act rightly as well as legally.
qs: regulators must move beyond categorical imperatives and blanket invocations of “core values” rhetoric to create “evidence-based regulation” that actually examines the merits of *both* “traditional” and “alternative” delivery models
we certainly should not leave the predictability, fairness, and individual rights at the heart of the rule of law solely to market forces.

every legal service provider will be evaluated on their ability to contribute to the creation of real solutions for clients, while also understanding its obligation to help to preserve the core values of the rule of law

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Wilkins and Esteban Ferrer predict partial job replacement by AI and machine learning, alongside continued human-intensive corporate legal services and greater collaboration with technology.
pts.d: The authors explicitly predict that AI and machine learning will replace some legal jobs, but do not specify occupations, numbers or a displacement rate. They envisage continued reliance on people who can work with new technologies and collaborate across professional boundaries. They consequently call for technology and data fluency, business literacy and cross-cultural adaptability alongside legal knowledge. Their broader market argument is that software competes with labor arbitrage as a cost-reduction mechanism and becomes embedded in law firms and legal departments, making technology vendors partners as well as potential substitutes. That broader argument concerns software generally, not exclusively AI. They identify AI and machine learning as areas in which legal startups seek to differentiate themselves, rather than claiming demonstrated superiority for those startups.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of literature synthesis and examples of technology adoption and organizational integration; the job-replacement prediction is not quantified or benchmarked.
pts.d: The authors give no direct empirical estimate supporting their prediction of AI-related job displacement. Their broader software-market analysis draws on Esteban’s 2017 review of 280 academic papers and professional reports, including 19 addressing technology companies’ service offerings. They explicitly treat citation frequency as a rough proxy for salience, not as evidence of adoption rates, effectiveness or labor displacement. Illustrative AI-related developments include Deloitte’s alliance with Kira Systems, Oracle’s January 2019 practice-management announcement and Elevate’s acquisition of Lex Predict. These examples establish the source’s account of investment and market positioning, not measured productivity or employment outcomes. The characterization of the Kira alliance as the largest professional-services AI deployment is attributed in the chapter to Kira CEO Noah Waisberg, not presented as the authors’ independently measured finding. The authors’ educational recommendations cite Heineman, Lee and Wilkins (2014).

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The chapter describes developments through early 2019 and projects continued change without a dated AI-displacement forecast.
pts.d: The AI job-replacement claim has no deadline; the accompanying qualification is that corporate legal delivery remains human-capital intensive for the foreseeable future. The broader integration trend is located after the global financial crisis and projected into 2019 and beyond. The authors do not predict the imminent disappearance of large law firms: they expect those firms to remain important, with prosperity linked to adaptive innovation and responsiveness to clients. They explicitly qualify the ability of any provider to deliver promised innovation or become a fully integrated solutions provider. These are qualifications to their overall transformation thesis rather than technical conditions for particular AI systems.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims primarily concern corporate legal providers, their workforces and sophisticated corporate buyers, with implications for legal education and regulation.
pts.d: Some unspecified legal jobs face replacement, while remaining lawyers and other professionals must gain technological and collaborative capabilities. Law schools are asked to teach complementary competencies. On the provider side, software vendors compete with labor-based outsourcing while also partnering with law firms and in-house departments; ALSPs delivering legal work remain distinct from vendors selling software. The Big Four’s legal businesses incorporate technology into broader integrated offerings. On the buyer side, corporate clients and legal departments seek efficient, commercially relevant solutions. The authors do not quantify gains for these clients or make a specific AI-based access-to-justice prediction. Their public-interest concern is that integration and market competition should not displace rule-of-law protections.
